videos.title: New Audi A2: here’s what I LOVED and HATED!
videos.summary_source_text:
New Audi A2: here’s what I LOVED and HATED! The Audi A2 is BACK… But is it as groundbreaking as the original? 

Explore new and used car deals with Carwow: https://bit.ly/Change-Your-Car-0709

Introducing the all-new Audi A2 e-tron! 

Audi has brought back the A2, and it’s set to replace the Audi A1 and Audi Q2! 

The question is: can this all-new Audi live up to the reputation of the original A2? And does it offer enough appeal over competitors like the Kia EV3 and Volvo EX30? Let’s take a closer look, starting with the design… 

Just like the original A2, the new model is relatively aerodynamic. Up front there’s a large, smooth panel that houses all of the safety driving features, and there are vents on either side of this to help smooth airflow around the car. There’s also a vent within the front bumper which can close to further help aero. Along the side you’ll find door handles similar to those on a Ferrari Purosangue, as well as more vents around the wheels and aero alloy wheels. Around the back, the similarities to the old car continue, along with large swooping taillights, a smart (and thin) Audi badge, coupled with a fake diffuser. 

On the inside, the main feature is the same swooping digital dial & infotainment screen - the same as found in any new Audi in 2026. Generally, materials are ok higher up in the cabin, with some cheaper plastics found when you reach lower down - although that’s to be expected with a car at this price point. Storage is ok throughout, and the seats are comfortable, with sports seats and Alcantara material available should you want it. The cupholder positioning can be moved, and there are buttons to open the door rather than traditional handles. 

The new Audi A2 e-tron will be available with 52, 61 and 84kWh battery packs. The entry-level car comes with 170hp & 350Nm, rising all the way to 326hp and 545Nm for the top-of-the-range model. The A2 offers ranges of 262 through to 401 miles, depending on which model you choose. 

The Audi A2 e-tron starts from £32,200, rising all the way up to £45,000 for the top-of-the-range model. This puts it slightly cheaper than the list price of its key competitors, but would you choose it over a Kia EV3 or Volvo EX30? Let us know in the comments!

videos.summary_source_text:
You're overlooking this simple thing Click link in bio for lowest price on the Ball First Board. The best ball strikers aren't swinging like a pendulum — they're creating a flat spot through impact that keeps the club level with the ground.

It’s one of the most direct indicators of what’s happening inside your digestive system.

🌟 Take the 2-minute Health Lever Quiz: https://drbrg.co/4gKEk8A

Just so you know, my full line of high-quality supplements is available on Amazon — search Dr. Berg Supplements.

And it can often point to potential issues long before they show up on other tests.

For example, if you notice your stool is thin, like a pencil or a cigar, that could signify a problem in your colon.

Small, hard pellets suggest something might be going on higher up in your digestive tract, perhaps affecting transit time.

And if your stool is consistently soft but not quite diarrhea, it might be an indication of missing gut microbes or even food allergies.

The color of your stool is also important. Light-colored or gray stool can point to a bile issue, which is produced by your liver and stored in your gallbladder.

If your stool has a bad odor and appears greasy, it might suggest a problem with your pancreas, as proper digestion of fats could be impaired.

It’s also important to know that it’s not normal to only have a bowel movement every 2 to 3 days. Ideally, you should have 1 to 2 bowel movements daily to ensure proper elimination.

Our bodies are constantly sending us signals like these.

videos.title: Claude Fable 5.1 vs Gemini 3.8 Flash: This Isn’t Even Close
videos.summary_source_text:
Claude Fable 5.1 vs Gemini 3.8 Flash: This Isn’t Even Close Link to our newsletter: https://bitbiased.ai/

Anthropic and Google just released competing AI models one day apart — but the biggest difference isn't intelligence. It's price. Gemini 3.8 Flash is roughly 13x cheaper per token than Claude Fable 5.1, while Anthropic's model is claiming major gains in deep reasoning, coding, and long-duration agentic work.

On September 1, 2026, Anthropic announced Claude Fable 5.1, calling it its most capable model yet for coding and difficult knowledge work. The next day, Google launched Gemini 3.8 Flash alongside Flash Cyber, a specialized cybersecurity variant. Google says this was its third Flash release in just six weeks.

That release cadence alone shows how dramatically the AI race has accelerated.

On Anthropic's own benchmarks, Fable 5.1 more than doubled its predecessor's agentic science score from 24.7% to 52.6%, while agentic coding increased from 42% to 55.8%. On Anthropic's long-duration coding benchmark, Fable 5.1 reached 73.4%, ahead of Opus 5 at 70%.

Anthropic also cut cache read pricing by 75% to $0.25 per million tokens — an important change for AI agents that repeatedly call a model during long-running tasks. Fable 5.1 supports a one-million-token context window, text, images, PDFs, and diagrams, but not video or audio. Standard pricing sits at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens.

Google took a very different approach.

Gemini 3.8 Flash launches at an introductory $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens. Google is competing on throughput and affordability without abandoning capability.

On DeepSWE, Gemini 3.8 Flash reportedly scored around 73.8%. Google's Harvey Legal Agent Benchmark increased from 8.8% with Gemini 3.7 Flash to 10.0%, while the specialized Flash Cyber model reportedly delivered a 2.6x improvement in correct patches on workloads from Google's Chrome security team.

Gemini 3.8 Flash also has a one-million-token context window, but supports text, images, PDFs, video, and audio — giving it an advantage for multimodal applications.

Head-to-head, the models represent two different strategies. Fable 5.1 appears stronger for deep multi-step reasoning, research-heavy work, and computer use, with Anthropic reporting a 77.9% partial-success score on OSWorld 2.0. Gemini 3.8 Flash reaches a reported 59.0%, up from 50.6% for Gemini 3.7 Flash.

But then there's the price gap.

At the announced rates, Gemini is roughly thirteen times cheaper per token. For a product processing 100 million tokens per day, the example explored in this video works out to roughly $6,000 per day with Fable 5.1 versus around $450 with Gemini 3.8 Flash.

For AI agents, that difference becomes even more important. Agents can make dozens or hundreds of model calls while planning, executing, testing, and correcting their work. Lower inference costs don't just make existing workflows cheaper — they can make entirely different levels of agentic computation economically practical.

Goldman Sachs projects AI-agent token consumption could increase 24x by 2030, while inference costs continue falling rapidly. If that trend holds, the winning AI model may not necessarily be the smartest one. It may be the model that's capable enough, fast enough, and cheap enough to run at enormous scale.

There's also an important limitation to this comparison: the benchmark numbers discussed here come from the companies themselves. At launch, there's no meaningful independent third-party verification directly comparing Fable 5.1 and Gemini 3.8 Flash under identical conditions.

So which one wins?

For deep research, complex reasoning, computer use, and demanding coding workflows, Fable 5.1 makes a strong case based on the reported results. For high-volume AI agents, multimodal applications, and products where inference cost matters at scale, Gemini 3.8 Flash becomes extremely difficult to ignore.

And that may be the real story: the AI race is shifting from finding one universally "best" model toward choosing the right model for the job.

videos.title: STOP, You're Training Your Biceps All Wrong!
videos.summary_source_text:
STOP, You're Training Your Biceps All Wrong! If you want to know how to build bigger biceps, how to get bigger biceps, or how to build big biceps that look thicker from every angle, this video shows you why simply doing more curls may not be the answer. You can perform barbell curls, dumbbell curls, preacher curls, hammer curls and cable curls every week, but if the mechanics are wrong, you can still leave biceps growth on the table.

Get the exact workouts and programs used by physical therapist Jeff Cavaliere here - https://athleanx.com
Subscribe To This Channel Here - http://bit.ly/2b0coMW

The biceps are not just elbow flexors. The biceps brachii also plays an important role in supinating the forearm, which means turning the palm upward. If you ignore that function and simply move a weight from the bottom of a curl to the top, you may be completing the rep without getting everything you can out of the muscle you are trying to build.

In this video, I break down the most common biceps training mistakes that can keep your arms from growing and show you how to fix the way you perform your curls.

One of the biggest mistakes is allowing other muscles to dominate the curl. When the shoulders drift forward, the elbows travel too far, the wrists bend excessively or momentum starts swinging the weight, the biceps can lose the tension you thought you were creating. Heavy curls are not automatically bad, but using more weight only helps if the target muscle is still doing the work.

Whether you are doing a barbell curl or dumbbell curl, think beyond simply getting the weight to your shoulders. Keep the tension where it belongs, control the eccentric on the way down, and use a range of motion that lets you challenge the biceps without turning the movement into a full-body exercise.

videos.title: 10 Prompts That Prove Gemini 3.8 Flash Is Next Level
videos.summary_source_text:
10 Prompts That Prove Gemini 3.8 Flash Is Next Level Link to our newsletter: https://bitbiased.ai/

Gemini 3.8 Flash scored nine points higher than 3.7 on one of Google’s coding benchmarks — but if you prompt it the same way you prompt every other AI model, you may barely notice the upgrade.

The biggest changes aren’t about fancy prompt engineering. Gemini 3.8 Flash is specifically better at finishing multi-step jobs, checking its own work, handling massive amounts of context, and operating more like an agent instead of stopping at the first plausible answer. The trick is knowing how to prompt those capabilities directly.

Released on September 2nd, 2026, just three weeks after Gemini 3.7 Flash, Google is positioning 3.8 Flash as its intelligent workhorse for coding, long-horizon reasoning, and autonomous agents. The benchmark improvements help explain why: DeepSWE reportedly climbed from roughly 65% to 74%, while TerminalBench jumped from around 82% to 91%.

And Google is pricing Gemini 3.8 Flash at under $1 per million input tokens, making the model particularly interesting for workloads where you need AI running repeatedly rather than answering an occasional question.

But those improvements don’t show up equally everywhere.

In this video, I break down the practical prompts that actually expose what Gemini 3.8 Flash is good at — without complicated prompt frameworks or massive system instructions.

We start with coding and one surprisingly important change: asking Gemini to test and fix its work before returning the final result. Instead of simply asking it to write code, you can define “done” as producing something that has already been checked. That plays directly into the model’s improvements on longer, multi-step tasks.

Then there’s reasoning. Gemini 3.8 Flash offers low, medium, and high thinking levels, with medium as the default. For problems involving real math, logic, or multi-part decisions, explicitly requesting high effort and step-by-step reasoning can make much more sense than using extra computation on a trivial question.

Current information is another important boundary. The script notes a training-data cutoff around March 2026, so for newer developments, asking Gemini to use web search can help ground the response in current sources instead of relying on model memory. That still doesn’t remove the need to verify the sources it provides.

We also look at prompting Gemini 3.8 Flash for multi-step planning: mapping dependencies, identifying tasks that require earlier work to be completed, and flagging decisions that need human approval rather than letting the model quietly make every assumption itself.

Then there’s context. With a context window exceeding one million tokens, Gemini 3.8 Flash can work with enormous transcripts and documents without forcing you to chop everything into tiny pieces. That opens up useful workflows like extracting action items, owners, and deadlines from an entire long meeting transcript in one pass.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is multimodal too, accepting images, video, audio, and PDFs as input. But there’s an important limitation: this model analyzes those inputs and responds with text; it isn’t itself an image, video, or audio generator.

And 3.8 isn’t better at everything. On Humanity’s Last Exam, the script notes a score of roughly 45%, essentially unchanged from 3.7. The biggest improvements appear concentrated around coding and structured multi-step work rather than every form of open-ended reasoning.

So the real lesson isn’t to make your prompts longer. It’s to define what “finished” means: test the code, check the answer, search for current information when needed, plan the entire task, and use the full context you have available.

Try one of your normal Gemini prompts twice — once normally, and once with an explicit instruction to check or test its answer before finishing — and compare what comes back.

CHAPTERS

00:00 The Gemini 3.8 Flash Prompting Difference
01:17 What Actually Changed, And Why It Decides Your Prompts
02:49 Getting It To Actually Finish The Job Instead Of Stopping Halfway
04:11 Getting It To Check Its Work Instead Of Guessing
05:17 Getting It To Pull Current Information Instead Of Guessing From Memory
06:19 Getting It To Plan Multi-Step Tasks Instead Of Answering One Piece At A Time
07:23 Getting It To Handle The Big Stuff Without Chopping It Up
08:25 Getting It To Actually Look At What You Hand It
09:25 Where It Still Falls Short
10:13 The Verdict

Stop Copying McDavid's Workout. Do This Instead. | The Train 2.0 Show Stop Copying McDavid's Workout. Do This Instead. | The Train 2.0 Show

Most hockey players build their summer around a program they saw an NHL player post, and then wonder why they show up to camp slower, tighter, or hurt. In this episode Kevin McKinnon, Train 2.0's Director of Coaching, sits down in person with Mason Hackel, a certified Train 2.0 coach and level three ATG coach out of Ann Arbor, to talk about the training philosophy he used to fix his own hips and what it looks like when you build it for a hockey player.

They get into the three lifts Mason builds every program around and the exact bodyweight standard he works players toward, the reason so many players tear an Achilles in the offseason and never see it coming, what to do about knee pain and hip pain before you touch anything explosive, the off-ice work that widens your corkscrew, one number in the gym that tracks directly with skating speed, and the order Kevin periodizes a summer so you peak at training camp instead of in July.

Watch the full episode for the standards, the demos, and the plan.

👉 Find Mason and every certified Train 2.0 coach on the coaches map: https://train2point0.com/coaches
👉 Mason Hackel: https://ability-training.com | Instagram: https://www.instagram.com/hockey_hacks_2.0/

The Downhill Skating System is the mechanics-first approach that unlocks effortless, controlled speed on the ice without extra conditioning, pushing or “trying harder.” Inspired by the movement signatures of players like Connor McDavid, Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar, Quinn Hughes, and other elite NHL skaters, this system teaches you how to move on the ice with gravity, using your body's own stretch shortening cycles mixed with the most efficient footwork patterns and various skating mechanics.

Most players skate “uphill”: stiff, blocky, pushing hard, creating tension and burning energy like we were always taught in traditional powerskating. Downhill skating flips that model. By using counter rotation, proper joint angles, and natural gravitational momentum, we teach you move faster with less effort.

Inside the Downhill Skating System, players learn to:

1) Unlock the inner spring for better acceleration.
2)Use different footwork patterns to add options, deception and effortlessness. 
3)Proper joint alignment for efficiency and balance instead of creating tension with push strides.

Apply NHL-base mechanics like shin angle, Y-angle, rhythm and cadence. Generate speed using the rocker, with heel pressure and subtle weight transfers.

This system is not what players would learn in traditional, outdated power skating methods. It’s a biomechanics-based operating system designed to match your body type and natural movement patterns.

Whether you’re trying to improve the forward stride, lateral movements, deception, or posture, Downhill Skating reveals the hidden mechanics the NHL’s best rely on, and shows you how to plug them into your game step by step.

If you’re ready to skate faster with less effort, flow through transitions, and move with the smoothness of the world’s best players, the Downhill Skating System is your blueprint to faster player development.

videos.title: What Happens When Hockey Players Stride With Gravity?
videos.summary_source_text:
What Happens When Hockey Players Stride With Gravity? The Downhill Skating System is the mechanics-first approach that unlocks effortless, controlled speed on the ice without extra conditioning, pushing or “trying harder.” Inspired by the movement signatures of players like Connor McDavid, Nathan MacKinnon, Cale Makar, Quinn Hughes, and other elite NHL skaters, this system teaches you how to move on the ice with gravity, using your body's own stretch shortening cycles mixed with the most efficient footwork patterns and various skating mechanics.

Most players skate “uphill”: stiff, blocky, pushing hard, creating tension and burning energy like we were always taught in traditional powerskating. Downhill skating flips that model. By using counter rotation, proper joint angles, and natural gravitational momentum, we teach you move faster with less effort.

Inside the Downhill Skating System, players learn to:

1) Unlock the inner spring for better acceleration.
2)Use different footwork patterns to add options, deception and effortlessness. 
3)Proper joint alignment for efficiency and balance instead of creating tension with push strides.

Apply NHL-base mechanics like shin angle, Y-angle, rhythm and cadence. Generate speed using the rocker, with heel pressure and subtle weight transfers.

This system is not what players would learn in traditional, outdated power skating methods. It’s a biomechanics-based operating system designed to match your body type and natural movement patterns.

Whether you’re trying to improve the forward stride, lateral movements, deception, or posture, Downhill Skating reveals the hidden mechanics the NHL’s best rely on, and shows you how to plug them into your game step by step.

If you’re ready to skate faster with less effort, flow through transitions, and move with the smoothness of the world’s best players, the Downhill Skating System is your blueprint to faster player development.

videos.summary_source_text:
Cover the Lead Side Like This  #golfswing #golftips To compress the ball well, your body needs to be preparing for impact earlier than most golfers realize. By allowing the lead shoulder to cover the lead leg and moving cohesively—shifting and turning together—you arrive at the impact line sooner and with more control. Using an alignment stick against the lead hip gives a clear visual of where impact should be and how early you can get there. This creates a smoother transition and much more consistent contact.

videos.title: Elon Musk’s “Macrohard” Is Supposed to Launch THIS MONTH
videos.summary_source_text:
Elon Musk’s “Macrohard” Is Supposed to Launch THIS MONTH Link to our newsletter: https://bitbiased.ai/

Elon Musk says Macrohard is still on track for a September 2026 launch. That deadline is now here — but behind the scenes, xAI’s ambitious “purely AI software company” has reportedly lost leaders, shed engineers, paused a roughly 600-person data operation, and effectively started over.

Macrohard began as a joke aimed at Microsoft. Musk teased the project in July 2025 as a “multi-agent AI software company,” and xAI filed a US trademark for the Macrohard name in August. Musk’s premise was surprisingly straightforward: because a company like Microsoft primarily produces software rather than physical hardware, its workflows could theoretically be simulated by AI agents.

The vision goes far beyond another Copilot. Musk described Grok spawning specialized coding and image agents capable of coordinating their work and evaluating outputs. In March 2026, he revealed more of the architecture: Grok would serve as the high-level “navigator,” while a Tesla-built agent watches a computer screen, clicks, types, and operates software like a human. Musk calls the combination Digital Optimus.

That immediately raised a bigger question: what happens if AI agents stop being assistants and start functioning as the workers themselves?

The economics help explain why Wall Street paid attention. A mid-level engineer can cost roughly $120,000 per year, while an Nvidia H100 GPU reportedly rents for around $3–$10 per hour. Behind xAI sits the enormous Colossus cluster in Memphis, reportedly containing more than 180,000 Nvidia GPUs. Macrohard also emerged as Anthropic pushed further into autonomous office work with Claude Cowork and Microsoft expanded Copilot across its ecosystem.

But the public pitch and the story unfolding inside xAI soon started looking very different.

Reports described Macrohard as stalled. Two leaders left in February. xAI co-founder Toby Pohlen was brought in to take over — and reportedly lasted just 16 days. More than 20 engineers publicly associated with Macrohard reportedly either left xAI or transferred elsewhere.

Then came another major setback: a data-labeling operation involving roughly 600 outside contractors was reportedly paused. Meanwhile, Tesla was developing its own computer-using agent, also unofficially called Digital Optimus, creating two teams inside Musk’s empire pursuing closely related ideas.

Musk responded by rebuilding. On March 12, xAI hired two senior engineers from Cursor, with both reporting directly to Musk. A day later, Musk acknowledged that Macrohard simply “wasn’t built right the first time.”

There’s also a wider xAI story underneath all of this. Roughly half of the company’s original 11 co-founders were reportedly gone, while some reporting put the SpaceX-integrated AI division’s operating loss above $2.5 billion for a single quarter. xAI has also reportedly leased excess Colossus capacity to competitors including Google and Anthropic.

One important distinction: some coverage initially characterized the Cursor move as an acquisition. What’s confirmed here is the hiring of two executives — not xAI purchasing Cursor.

Now September 2026 has arrived.

The Macrohard trademark is real. Musk has publicly described the architecture. xAI has continued recruiting for roles connected to the project, including AI agent testing and data-labeling jobs reportedly paying up to $40 per hour.

What we still don’t have is a working public demo, a shipped public product, or independent verification that the rebuilt team has solved the coordination and reliability problems that reportedly derailed the first version.

So does Musk actually deliver Macrohard this month? Do we get a full public launch, a limited release designed to technically hit the deadline, another delay — or nothing at all?

This video reconstructs the full Macrohard story and separates what’s confirmed from what remains a promise.

videos.title: OpenAI cuts off Musk, Anthropic BEATS Pentagon, Grok could go DARK: AI NEWS
videos.summary_source_text:
OpenAI cuts off Musk, Anthropic BEATS Pentagon, Grok could go DARK: AI NEWS Link to our newsletter: https://bitbiased.ai/

OpenAI is reportedly cutting off model access to Cursor after SpaceX announced a $60 billion acquisition of Anysphere. A federal judge just ruled that the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic was illegal and baseless. And xAI has warned a court that an environmental dispute over gas turbines could cause Grok to largely cease functioning for hundreds of millions of users.

Three stories that look completely unrelated are really asking the same question: who actually controls whether an AI model gets to keep running?

The first fight centers on Cursor, the AI coding tool built by Anysphere. After SpaceX announced it was acquiring the company in a deal reportedly worth $60 billion, OpenAI moved to cut off Cursor’s access to its models, with the cutoff scheduled for November 12. According to the reporting discussed in this video, OpenAI’s justification involves distrust of Musk-connected companies alongside alleged terms-of-service violations tied to xAI.

But that explanation has two very different layers. A terms-of-service violation is something concrete. Distrust of companies connected to Elon Musk is much broader. And when the decision arrives within days of one of OpenAI’s best-funded competitors acquiring Cursor, the move becomes more than a simple compliance story.

There is also an important limitation: we do not yet have a public, itemized breakdown showing exactly which terms were allegedly violated and when. That makes this potentially both a policy enforcement decision and a strategic competitive move.

Then there is Anthropic.

Earlier in 2026, the Department of Defense pushed Anthropic to remove two restrictions governing military use of Claude: its prohibition on autonomous weapons selecting targets without human involvement and its prohibition on mass domestic surveillance of Americans. Anthropic refused.

The Pentagon subsequently designated Anthropic under a federal statute that legal experts described as having never previously been used against a domestic American company and as normally being associated with foreign sabotage threats. Anthropic sued in March.

Now a federal judge has ruled that the Pentagon’s blacklisting of Anthropic was illegal and baseless.

That could reopen the path toward military contracts potentially worth billions, but it does not mean those contracts automatically return. The Pentagon can still appeal, and existing arrangements involving competitors including OpenAI and xAI remain unaffected. What changed is Anthropic’s legal position after months of fighting one of the most powerful customers in the world over how Claude could be used.

And then the third story moves from model access and military policy to something much more physical: electricity.

xAI is facing a Clean Air Act lawsuit involving gas turbines at a Mississippi power site that the suit alleges were not properly permitted. Those turbines help support the compute infrastructure behind Grok.

In a federal court filing, xAI argued that shutting down that power source could cause Grok to largely cease functioning for hundreds of millions of users.

That is an enormous claim, but it needs context. It comes from xAI itself during active litigation in which the company is attempting to avoid an injunction. It should therefore be understood as a legal argument rather than an independently verified assessment that Grok is actually on the verge of going offline.

Put all three stories together and the bigger pattern becomes clear.

OpenAI can control access to the models another company depends on. Anthropic just fought over how much leverage the Pentagon can exercise over an AI provider that refuses certain uses of its technology. And xAI is arguing that regulators’ control over physical power infrastructure could ultimately determine whether Grok stays available.

Same lever. Three different hands trying to hold it.

The most important AI battles may increasingly have less to do with benchmark scores and model capabilities and more to do with access agreements, government contracts, courts, infrastructure, electricity, and who ultimately controls the switch.

And none of these stories is finished yet. The Cursor cutoff has not taken effect. The Pentagon can still appeal the Anthropic ruling. And xAI’s turbine dispute remains in litigation.

The models themselves may not have changed this week. The power structures determining whether people can use them did.

CHAPTERS

03:49 The Court Just Overturned the Pentagon Ban
06:02 xAI Says Grok Could Go Dark
08:00 What Actually Connects These Three Stories
09:01 The Limitations Nobody Is Putting in the Thumbnail
10:11 The Verdict

videos.title: The Golf Swing Becomes Effortless When You Understand This
videos.summary_source_text:
The Golf Swing Becomes Effortless When You Understand This Ever wondered why your golf swing can feel so difficult… when your body is actually capable of producing an incredible golf swing naturally?

I recently came across a video from Christian Cee  that stopped me in my tracks.

One moment he was making a fairly typical amateur golf swing. Seconds later, without even realising it, he produced a movement that looked remarkably similar to some of the best golfers in the world.

The interesting part?

Nobody taught him how to do it.

In this golf lesson, Danny Maude reveals why Christian’s accidental “tour level” movement happened — and what it can teach you about creating a more natural, powerful and effortless golf swing.

Most golfers spend their time trying to control individual parts of the swing.

Where should my hands go?
How should my hips move?
Am I shifting my weight correctly?
Where should the club be at impact?

But your body is incredibly good at organising movement when you give it a clear enough task.

Christian accidentally demonstrated this perfectly.

He created weight shift, rotation, extension, speed and a powerful release without consciously trying to manufacture any of them.

The challenge is learning how to bring that same freedom into your golf swing… while still controlling the clubface and striking the golf ball consistently.

In this video you’ll discover:

• Why Christian accidentally created a golf swing that looked like a tour professional
• How your body naturally organises movement around a clear task
• Why focusing too much on the golf ball can actually make your swing worse
• The difference between your primary and secondary targets in the golf swing
• How to combine freedom with control
• A simple ball throwing drill inspired by Pete Cowen
• How to improve your strike without becoming obsessed with impact
• Why trying to “control” your golf swing can often make you lose control
• A simple stepping exercise that can help develop a more natural golf swing
• How to build trust and create effortless speed through impact

The goal isn’t to stop caring about your strike.

It’s to stop making the golf ball the master of your entire movement.

When you learn to connect what’s happening at impact with where you actually want the golf club and golf ball to go, the swing can start to organise itself very differently.

And often, many of the movements golfers spend years trying to manufacture begin to appear naturally.

Statin medications are the most commonly prescribed drug class in the United States, yet most people are unaware of their potential side effects.

Statins are typically prescribed when cholesterol levels are high. They block the production of cholesterol, but they also block the production of CoQ10, which is vital for muscle and heart health.

If you’re taking statins, CoQ10 can help mitigate the side effects. Ubiquinol is a fast-acting form of CoQ10 and may be the best form to take. A typical amount is 200–400 mg.

Instead of immediately taking statins, ask yourself: Why do you have high cholesterol in the first place? Refined carbohydrates and sugar can contribute to cholesterol production in the body. Low bile, gallbladder problems, or gallbladder removal can also contribute to high cholesterol.
